entries: Acids and alkalis around you - lemon juice and vinegar are acids, soap and baking soda are alkalis, and chemists sort them all on the pH scale.
slots.label: Around you
slots.studentPrompt: Explain this step in your own words.

entries: The pH scale ladder - the scale runs from 0 to 14 with 7 neutral, and each step away from 7 is ten times stronger.
slots.label: The ladder
slots.studentPrompt: Explain this step in your own words.

entries: What pH is really about: ions - acids release H+ ions and alkalis release OH- ions in water, and whichever ion is in excess decides the pH.
slots.label: Ions
slots.studentPrompt: Explain this step in your own words.

entries: Neutralisation: a worked example - H+ and OH- ions pair up to make water, and the leftover ions form a salt: acid plus alkali gives salt plus water.
slots.label: Neutralisation
slots.studentPrompt: Explain this step in your own words.

entries: The litmus test - blue litmus turns red in acid and red litmus turns blue in alkali; no change means neutral.
slots.label: Litmus test
slots.studentPrompt: Explain this step in your own words.

entries: Naming the salt - hydrochloric acid gives a chloride, nitric acid a nitrate, and sulfuric acid a sulfate.
slots.label: Naming the salt
slots.studentPrompt: Explain this step in your own words.

entries: A common mistake: all acids are strong - a weak acid only partly releases its hydrogen ions, so vinegar is acidic without being strong.
slots.label: Weak acids
slots.studentPrompt: Explain this step in your own words.

entries: The titration curve: watch for the jump - base added drop by drop moves the pH slowly, then one drop leaps it from 4 to 10 at the equivalence point, where the indicator must change colour.
slots.label: The jump
slots.studentPrompt: Explain this step in your own words.

entries: The 0 to 14 scale that measures acidity and alkalinity: below 7 is acidic, 7 is neutral, above 7 is alkaline, and each step is ten times stronger.
slots.label: pH scale
slots.studentPrompt: Give your own example of this term.

entries: A substance that releases hydrogen ions, H+, when dissolved in water. Acids have a pH below 7.
slots.label: Acid
slots.studentPrompt: Give your own example of this term.

entries: A substance that releases hydroxide ions, OH-, when dissolved in water. Alkalis have a pH above 7 and are soluble bases.
slots.label: Alkali
slots.studentPrompt: Give your own example of this term.

entries: A hydrogen ion released by an acid in water. The more H+ ions in excess, the lower the pH.
slots.label: Hydrogen ion
slots.studentPrompt: Give your own example of this term.

entries: A hydroxide ion released by an alkali in water. The more OH- ions in excess, the higher the pH.
slots.label: Hydroxide ion
slots.studentPrompt: Give your own example of this term.

entries: The reaction of an acid with an alkali, in which H+ and OH- ions pair up to form water and the leftover ions form a salt.
slots.label: Neutralisation
slots.studentPrompt: Give your own example of this term.

entries: The ionic compound left over after neutralisation. Its second name comes from the acid: chloride, nitrate or sulfate.
slots.label: Salt
slots.studentPrompt: Give your own example of this term.

entries: A dye that changes colour in acid and alkali, used to test pH. Litmus turns red in acid and blue in alkali.
slots.label: Indicator
slots.studentPrompt: Give your own example of this term.

entries: Adding a solution drop by drop from a burette to find exactly how much is needed to neutralise the other solution.
slots.label: Titration
slots.studentPrompt: Give your own example of this term.

entries: The point in a titration where the acid and alkali have exactly reacted, shown by the vertical jump on the pH curve.
slots.label: Equivalence point
slots.studentPrompt: Give your own example of this term.

entries: An acid that only partly releases its hydrogen ions in water, such as the acid in vinegar. It is still acidic, just not strong.
slots.label: Weak acid
slots.studentPrompt: Give your own example of this term.
